name: Heaps & Priority Queue Algorithms
tagline: A complete binary (or d-ary) tree packed in a contiguous array maintaining heap-order in O(log n) updates and O(1) min/max peek.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of binary and d-ary heaps—from Floyd's O(n) bottom-up heapify and cache-friendly array layout to streaming Top-K and indexed vs. lazy-deletion heaps.

spark.summary: A binary heap is a complete binary tree packed into a contiguous array that maintains the heap-order invariant in O(log n) per update and O(1) for min/max inspection.
spark.keyTakeaway: Packing a complete tree into a flat array gives O(log n) priority operations with L1-cache-friendly memory access, making binary and 4-ary heaps faster in practice than theoretically tighter pointer-based heaps.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** A **binary heap** is a complete binary tree stored implicitly inside a flat contiguous array—zero left/right/parent pointers needed! Node `i`'s parent sits at `(i - 1) >> 1` and its children sit at `2*i + 1` and `2*i + 2`.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Min-Heap Array Layout: Parent=(i-1)>>1, Children=2i+1, 2i+2 (idx 0 : min=2 -> idx 1 : val=5 -> idx 2 : val=8 -> idx 3:12); Indexed Heap decreaseKey vs. Lazy-Deletion Bloat (Dijkstra Loop -> pos[nodeId] Map -> 4-ary Heap[<=V]).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Cache locality beats asymptotic pointer tricks in real hardware. On dense graphs (`|E| >> |V|`), lazy deletion in Dijkstra can bloat the heap to `O(E)` entries.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Practice streaming Top-K, sliding-window monotonic deques, and shortest-path/MST algorithms.

learningJourney.title: What is a Binary Heap
learningJourney.explanation:
A **binary heap** is a complete binary tree stored implicitly inside a flat contiguous array—zero left/right/parent pointers needed! Node `i`'s parent sits at `(i - 1) >> 1` and its children sit at `2*i + 1` and `2*i + 2`.

In a **min-heap**, every parent is `<=` its children (`heap[0]` is always the global minimum). Inserting appends to the end and calls `siftUp` (`O(log n)`); popping swaps `heap[0]` with the last element and calls `siftDown` (`O(log n)`).

sectionDiagram.title: Min-Heap Array Layout: Parent=(i-1)>>1, Children=2i+1, 2i+2

cards.label: Zero Pointers
cards.detail: Saves 16–24 bytes per node vs. pointer trees and keeps levels contiguous in L1/L2 cache.

cards.label: O(n) Heapify
cards.detail: Floyd's bottom-up siftDown from n//2 - 1 down to 0 builds a heap in O(n), not O(n log n).

cards.label: 4-ary Heaps
cards.detail: Fitting 4 children in one 64-byte cache line cuts tree height in half for Dijkstra.

sectionDiagram.summary: Implicit array indexing turns a complete binary tree into a cache-friendly O(log n) priority queue.

learningJourney.title: Why Dynamic Priority Streams Beat Re-Sorting
learningJourney.explanation: Re-sorting an array on every insert costs `O(n log n)` per event. In an observability pipeline ingesting 500,000 latency records/sec that needs the 50 slowest endpoints, a fixed-size `k=50` min-heap compares each event against `heap[0]` in `O(1)`—rejecting `99.9%` of events immediately and using just `O(k)` memory.

ideas.title: Floyd's O(n) Bottom-Up Heapify
ideas.description: Half the nodes are leaves needing 0 swaps; running `siftDown` from `n//2 - 1` down to `0` sums to `< 2n` comparisons.

ideas.title: Indexed Heap vs. Lazy Deletion
ideas.description: Standard `heapq`/`PriorityQueue` lack `decreaseKey`. Maintain a parallel `pos[id]` map for true `O(log n)` in-place updates, or push duplicates and skip stale pops.

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Why Dynamic Priority Streams Beat Re-Sorting under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Where Heaps Excel (and Where BSTs or Quickselect Win)
learningJourney.explanation: Heaps optimize repeated min/max extraction from changing streams; they do not support arbitrary search or range queries.

benefits: `O(n log k)` streaming Top-K in `O(k)` RAM; `O((V+E) log V)` shortest-path frontier extraction.
costs: Mutating priority keys in-place without an indexed map or re-pushing corrupts the heap invariant.

comparison.choice: Avoid: Arbitrary Search or Range Queries (`x <= k <= y`)
benefits: Balanced BSTs (B-tree, Red-Black tree) or skip lists support `O(log n)` predecessor/range lookups.
costs: Finding an arbitrary element inside a heap requires an `O(n)` linear scan.

benefits: `quickselect` finds the k-th element in `O(n)` expected time without maintaining a heap.
costs: Building and popping a heap on static data adds unnecessary `O(n log k)` work.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: Streaming Top-K Min-Heap with Monotonic Tie-Breaker
learningJourney.explanation: Include a monotonic sequence counter `(score, seq_id, item)` if deterministic FIFO tie-breaking is required, and guard against integer overflow in custom comparators by using explicit `<` / `>` instead of `a - b`.
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Binary Heap vs. 4-ary Heap vs. Fibonacci Heap
learningJourney.explanation: Cache locality beats asymptotic pointer tricks in real hardware.

benefits: Simple, 2 child comparisons per level, built into Python `heapq` and Java `PriorityQueue`.
costs: No native `O(log n)` `decreaseKey` without an external `pos[id]` index map.

benefits: Halves tree height (`log_4 n`) and fits 4 children into one 64-byte CPU cache line—ideal for Dijkstra.
costs: 4 child comparisons per `siftDown` level make `pop` slightly more work.
Pointer chasing causes severe L1/L2 cache misses, making it slower in practice than 4-ary heaps.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production Guard: Indexed Heap Preventing Lazy-Deletion Bloat
learningJourney.explanation: On dense graphs (`|E| >> |V|`), lazy deletion in Dijkstra can bloat the heap to `O(E)` entries. An **indexed heap** maintains `pos[nodeId]` on every swap so `decreaseKey` updates the existing slot in-place, keeping heap size strictly `<= V`.

sectionDiagram.title: Indexed Heap decreaseKey vs. Lazy-Deletion Bloat
sectionDiagram.summary: Maintaining pos[nodeId] on every swap bounds heap memory strictly to O(V) even on dense graphs.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the time complexity of building a valid binary heap from an unsorted array of `N` elements using Floyd's bottom-up `heapify`?

options.text: `O(N)` — because half the nodes are leaves needing 0 swaps and most others sit near the bottom
`O(N log N)` — because every element must travel from the leaf to the root
options.feedback: Top-down repeated `push` is `O(N log N)`, whereas bottom-up `siftDown` is `O(N)`.

options.text: `O(log N)` — because only the root needs to be sifted
options.feedback: All `N/2` internal nodes must be sifted down.
